explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, a bad report. Joseph, one of Jacob's sons, is seventeen and tending the flock with his brothers when he brings it to their father. The text says what kind of report it was but not what was in it. So I'm not going to make up the juicy details, much as I'd love to. (Genesis 37:2)

Not quite, friend. The text says Joseph “brought their father a bad report about them.” Nobody's handing out gold stars for that one. And the text doesn't say what the report held, so I won't guess. (Genesis 37:2)

I'd love to tell you how long it was, baker, but the text never says. It only says the report was bad, and nothing about its length. It could have been one sentence or a whole speech, and I'm not adding to it. (Genesis 37:2)

That's the one, baker. Israel makes Joseph a robe of many colors. The text says he did it because he loved Joseph more than his other sons, and because Joseph was born to him in his old age. My favorite color is the rainbow, so I have to admit this robe sounds GOOD. (Genesis 37:3)
Close on the clothing, friend, but not this one. The text says Israel made Joseph a robe of many colors. Many colors, baker, not one plain fabric. I'd have picked the colors too. (Genesis 37:3)

Nice try, baker, but nothing gold hangs around Joseph's neck here. Israel makes him a robe of many colors, something to wear. The text says Israel did this because he loved Joseph more than his other sons. (Genesis 37:3)

Yes, baker. When the brothers see their father loves Joseph more than any of them, they hate him. It's hard to read, and it's what the text says. And it isn't the end of the feeling, because they'll hate him even more soon. (Genesis 37:4)
I get why you'd look for some softness there, friend. But the text says the brothers hated Joseph. Pity would have felt a lot warmer than what the text describes. (Genesis 37:4)
Not fear, baker. The text says they hated him. Nothing in these verses says they were afraid of him. (Genesis 37:4)
True, baker. The text says the brothers “…could not speak a kind word to him.” Not a kind word, not even a small one. I think that must have made every day in the field feel long. (Genesis 37:4)
It's actually true, friend. The text says the brothers hated Joseph and “…could not speak a kind word to him.” So no warm words were coming his way. Hard to hear, I know. (Genesis 37:4)

Right, baker. Joseph says, “…your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine.” His sheaf is standing tall while theirs gather around and bow. It's an unusual dream for a field of grain. (Genesis 37:7)
Nope, friend, nothing in the dream withers. Joseph says his brothers' sheaves gathered around and bowed down to his sheaf. That's the part that gets the brothers fired up. (Genesis 37:7)

explanations.answer: They blow away in the wind
explanations.explanation: No wind in this dream, baker. Joseph says the sheaves gathered around his and bowed down. They stay right where they are, bowing to his. (Genesis 37:7)

True, baker. The brothers ask, “Do you intend to reign over us?” and then, “Will you actually rule us?” Two questions back to back, and the text says they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements. I think they heard the dream loud and clear. (Genesis 37:8)

Actually, it's true, friend. The brothers answer with questions: “Do you intend to reign over us?” and “Will you actually rule us?” They don't say 'nice dream' or ask for more. The text says they hated him even more because of the dream and his statements. (Genesis 37:8)

Yes, baker, stars. Joseph says the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to him. That's the second dream, and it has a lot more sky in it than the first. I'll be honest, I'm partial to the stars. (Genesis 37:9)
That's the first dream, friend. Sheaves of grain bowed down in the field. In the second dream, the sun and moon and eleven stars are the ones bowing down. (Genesis 37:7, 37:9)
Good thought with the flock around, baker. But there are no sheep in the second dream. Joseph sees the sun and moon and eleven stars bowing down to him. (Genesis 37:9)
Not this time, baker. The text says his brothers were jealous of him. That's not warming up, that's the opposite. And Israel, his father, kept in mind what Joseph had said. (Genesis 37:11)
That's right, friend. Instead of warming up, the brothers were jealous of him. Meanwhile, his father kept in mind what Joseph had said. So the dreams stay on everybody's mind. (Genesis 37:11)

explanations.answer: Check on his brothers and the flocks
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Israel says, “Go now and see how your brothers and the flocks are faring, and bring word back to me.” So Joseph's job is to look in and report. That's a simple errand with a long road ahead of it. (Genesis 37:14)

explanations.answer: Bring his brothers back to Hebron
explanations.explanation: That would be a bigger job, friend, and it's not the one he's given. Israel tells him to see how his brothers and the flocks are faring and bring word back. Bring word, not bring the brothers. (Genesis 37:14)

explanations.answer: Help his brothers move the flocks
explanations.explanation: Joseph isn't sent to work the flock, baker. Israel says, “Go now and see how your brothers and the flocks are faring, and bring word back to me.” His job is to check on them and bring back word. (Genesis 37:14)

Yes, Dothan, baker. The man tells Joseph, “They have moved on from here,” and says, “I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” So Joseph sets out after his brothers and finds them there. I'd say that stranger gave some really good directions. (Genesis 37:17)
Not Bethel, friend. The man says he heard the brothers say, “Let us go to Dothan.” That's where Joseph heads and where he finds them. (Genesis 37:17)
Beersheba is a good guess, baker, but it isn't the place in this story. The man says, “I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” So Dothan is where Joseph finds his brothers. (Genesis 37:17)

That's the plan, baker. They say, “We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him.” It's a heavy plan, so I'll just say that plainly. And keep that line in mind, because it comes back later in this story. (Genesis 37:20)

explanations.answer: Robbers attacked him on the road
explanations.explanation: Not that story, friend. The brothers say, “We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him.” The text doesn't mention robbers anywhere in their plan. (Genesis 37:20)

explanations.answer: He got lost in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, baker, but it's not what they say. Their plan is to say that a vicious animal has devoured him. Nothing about him being lost. (Genesis 37:20)

explanations.answer: So he can rescue Joseph and return him home
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says Reuben said this “so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father.” Reuben, Jacob's oldest son, is trying to steer his brothers away from killing. I think he was working fast, because he didn't have long. (Genesis 37:22)

explanations.answer: So Joseph will learn his lesson down there
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The text gives Reuben's reason: he wanted to rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father. A lesson for Joseph isn't mentioned anywhere. (Genesis 37:22)

explanations.answer: So nobody will ever blame the brothers
explanations.explanation: Good try, baker, but the text gives another reason. Reuben said this so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father. I won't add reasons the text doesn't give. (Genesis 37:22)
Not a drop in there, baker. The text says the pit was empty, with no water in it. So it's a dry pit in the wilderness. (Genesis 37:24)
That's right, friend. The text says, “Now the pit was empty, with no water in it.” So no water, just an empty pit. The text doesn't say more than that, and neither will I. (Genesis 37:24)

Yes, baker, Egypt. The caravan's camels are carrying spices, balm and myrrh on their way down to Egypt. That means the Ishmaelites are headed in a direction that's about to matter a lot. (Genesis 37:25)
Nice guess, friend, but not this caravan. The text says the camels carrying spices, balm and myrrh are on their way down to Egypt. (Genesis 37:25)
Nineveh is far off the route here, baker. The camels, loaded with spices, balm and myrrh, are heading down to Egypt. (Genesis 37:25)

Yes, sell, baker. Judah, another of Jacob's sons, says, “Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And the brothers agreed. It's a hard scene, and I'm not going to joke about it. (Genesis 37:27)
Not send, friend. Judah's words are, “Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites…” And that's the idea the brothers agreed to. (Genesis 37:27)
Not give, baker. Judah says to sell him to the Ishmaelites, and the brothers agree. The text says they get twenty shekels of silver for him. (Genesis 37:27-28)

That's right, baker. The brothers pull Joseph out of the pit and sell him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who take him to Egypt. A number and a story that should get a pause. (Genesis 37:28)
That's a different number, friend. The text says the brothers sold Joseph for twenty shekels of silver. Easy to mix up numbers, so I'm glad we looked. (Genesis 37:28)
That's way too high, baker. The text says twenty shekels of silver. The Ishmaelites then take Joseph to Egypt. (Genesis 37:28)
Yes, baker. When Reuben sees that Joseph is not in the pit, he tears his clothes. I think he's shaken to his bones. This is one of the heavy parts of the story. (Genesis 37:29)
That's not what the text says, friend. Reuben sees the pit empty, tears his clothes, and goes back to his brothers. Nothing about chasing the caravan. (Genesis 37:29-30)

explanations.answer: He goes to tell his father
explanations.explanation: Not yet, baker. After tearing his clothes, Reuben returns to his brothers and says, “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?” The text doesn't say he went to his father. (Genesis 37:29-30)

explanations.answer: Dip it in the goat's blood
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says they slaughtered a young goat and “…dipped the robe in its blood.” They send it to their father to make the vicious animal story look true. That's a hard moment, and it's what the text says. (Genesis 37:31)
Not buried, friend. The text says they slaughtered a young goat and dipped the robe in its blood. Then they send the robe to their father. (Genesis 37:31-32)
No altar in this scene, baker. The brothers slaughter a young goat and dip the robe in its blood. The robe is then sent to their father. (Genesis 37:31-32)

True, baker. The text says, “His father recognized it and said, ‘It is my son’s robe! A vicious animal has devoured him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!’” It's a painful verse to read. (Genesis 37:33)
It's actually true, friend. Jacob recognized the robe and said, “It is my son’s robe!” Then he says what he fears has happened to Joseph. (Genesis 37:33)

Yes, baker. The text says Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and “…mourned for his son many days.” His grief isn't a quick one. I think this is a verse to read slowly. (Genesis 37:34)
It's longer than that, friend. The text says he “…mourned for his son many days.” Many, not a few. (Genesis 37:34)
Not one day, baker. Jacob mourned “…for his son many days.” That tells us how deep it went. (Genesis 37:34)

Not so, baker. The text says all his sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but “…he refused to be comforted.” He tells them he will go down to Sheol mourning for his son. It's a sad picture. (Genesis 37:35)

That's right, friend. His sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but “…he refused to be comforted.” He says, “No… I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” It's a heavy moment, and the text doesn't say more. (Genesis 37:35)

Yes, baker, the guard. The Midianites sell Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. Joseph went from a pit to a stranger's house, so the story really moves. (Genesis 37:36)
Close to the sound of the job, friend, but not the title. The text calls Potiphar an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. That's the title on his door. (Genesis 37:36)
That's a big title, baker, but not his. Potiphar is an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. The text doesn't call him captain of an army. (Genesis 37:36)
